title: Writing a news report
examples: How do I write a catchy headline?
What is the difference between the five Ws and the main story?
Should I put the most important information first?

explain.say: Today we are learning to write a news report.

items: It should grab the reader's attention.
It tells the main idea quickly.

explain.say: Next we need to cover the five Ws of journalism.

draw.text: The Five Ws: Who, What, Where, When, Why

explain.say: The inverted pyramid is how we structure the story.
Every news report must answer the five Ws right away.

items: Step 2: Write the lead answering the 5 Ws.

explain.say: For example, if a puppy was found in the park yesterday, that is a news story.

draw.text: Example: Puppy found in local park

explain.say: A common mistake is putting the least important detail first.

faq.q: What exactly does 'inverted pyramid' mean for my writing?
faq.a: It means you put the most important facts right at the very beginning of your report. You save the less important details for later in the article.
asks: How should I order my news story?
Does the order matter in a news report?

faq.q: Do I have to include all five Ws in the first paragraph?
faq.a: Yes, trying to answer Who, What, Where, When, and Why in your opening paragraph is very important. This grabs the reader right away.
asks: What are the five Ws again?
Should I answer all five questions in the lead?

faq.q: How long should a headline be?
faq.a: A good headline should be short and punchy, but it must still tell the reader what the article is about. Think of it like a catchy title.

faq.q: Can I use the five Ws if I don't know all the answers?
faq.a: If you are reporting on something, try to find as many of the five Ws as possible. If you are missing one, you can mention that the information is still coming.
asks: What if I don't know the 'Why'?
Is it okay to miss one of the Ws?

faq.q: Is the headline the same as the main topic sentence?
faq.a: No, the headline is just a short title for the whole piece. The main topic sentence is usually the first sentence inside the report itself.
asks: Is the headline the same as the first sentence?
What is the difference between the title and the lead?

facts: A headline must be catchy and summarize the main event.
The five Ws are Who, What, Where, When, and Why.
The inverted pyramid places the most crucial information at the beginning.
The lead paragraph should attempt to answer all five Ws.

quiz.say: The most important facts should appear:
quiz.why: The inverted pyramid structure requires the most vital information to be presented first so the reader knows the main point immediately.

wrong.0: This is tempting because the middle section holds important details, but the absolute most crucial facts must come first.
wrong.1: This is wrong because if you wait until the end, the reader might lose interest before finding the main point.
wrong.2: The headline is a summary, but the full details and answers to the Ws must be written out in the lead paragraph.

quiz.say: If you are writing about a lost dog, which W answers the question 'Who was involved'?
quiz.why: The 'Who' always refers to the people or animals involved in the event, like the dog and the person who found it.

wrong.2: This describes the 'What', not the people or animals involved.

quiz.say: What is the main purpose of a headline?

options.show: To give all the background details
options.say: To give all the background details

options.show: To ask a question to the reader
options.say: To ask a question to the reader

options.show: To grab attention and summarize the story
options.say: To grab attention and summarize the story

quiz.why: A headline acts like a hook; it must be exciting enough to make the reader want to read the full report.

wrong.0: Background details belong lower down in the article, not in the headline.
wrong.1: While some headlines are questions, their main job is to state the core event, not just ask something.
wrong.2: News reports must be factual and neutral; the headline should report, not argue.
